title: Roads, Rules and Traffic Lights
summary: Early cars bumped along muddy, dusty roads built for horses. People learned to glue roads together with tar, built highways right across whole countries, and invented traffic lights, stop signs, driving tests and number plates to keep everyone safe. They even had to invent the gas station!

sections.heading: Mud, Dust and Mr McAdam
paragraphs: At the end of the last part, millions of new cars were rolling out of factories. But a car is only as good as the road under its wheels, and in 1900 most roads were terrible. In the countryside of Europe and America, a typical road was simply a strip of packed earth. In dry weather it was rutted and bumpy. After rain it turned into a sticky brown soup that could swallow a wheel up to the axle. Horses could plod through mud. Early cars, with their thin tires and weak engines, often could not.

The best roads of the time owed a great deal to a Scottish engineer born almost a hundred years before the first car. John Loudon McAdam (1756–1836) had made money in business in New York as a young man, then returned to Scotland and became a trustee of a turnpike, a road whose users paid a toll to keep it in repair. He was fascinated, and annoyed, by how badly roads were built. In 1816 he became surveyor of roads for the turnpike trust around Bristol in England, in charge of about 149 miles of road, and he started testing his ideas for real.

McAdam's idea was surprisingly simple. Earlier engineers, like the Romans, had built roads on thick, expensive foundations of big stones. McAdam said you did not need that. The natural soil could carry the weight, as long as you kept it dry. So he raised the road a little above the surrounding ground and gave it a gentle hump in the middle, called a camber, so that rainwater ran off into ditches at the sides. On a road 30 feet (about 9 metres) wide, the middle stood only about 3 inches (7.5 cm) higher than the edges.

On top of the soil went layers of broken stone. The lower layer was about 20 cm thick, made of stones up to about 7.5 cm across. The top layer was thinner, about 5 cm, made of small stones about 2 cm across. Size really mattered. McAdam's workers broke stones by hand with hammers, and supervisors were told to check that no stone weighed more than about 6 ounces (170 grams). A popular saying, often linked to McAdam, was that any stone too big to fit in your mouth was too big for the road. The sharp, angular pieces locked together like a jigsaw as wheels rolled over them, making a hard, smooth crust.

From about 1820 his method spread quickly, and his name became a word: a road built this way was 'macadamised', or simply 'macadam'. In 1823 the first macadam road in the United States was finished in Maryland, on a 10-mile stretch between Hagerstown and Boonsboro. Before it was rebuilt, a winter stagecoach could take five to seven hours to cover those 10 miles. That gives you an idea of how slow travel on bad roads could be.

Macadam worked brilliantly for horses and iron-rimmed carriage wheels. Then the car arrived, and something unexpected happened. A fast-moving rubber tire creates a little pocket of low air pressure behind it, and this sucks the fine dust out from between the stones. Every car that sped along a macadam road dragged a huge cloud of dust behind it. People living by the road had dust in their houses and lungs. Worse still, as the dust was pulled away, the stones lost their grip on each other and the road slowly fell apart.

The answer was to glue the stones together. In 1902 a Swiss doctor, Ernest Guglielminetti, suggested spraying tar from the gasworks in Monaco onto the roads to hold the dust down. Around the same time a Welsh-born engineer, Edgar Purnell Hooley (1860–1942), was county surveyor for Nottinghamshire in England. According to the story he later told, in 1901 he walked past a tar works and noticed a spot where a barrel of tar had spilled and someone had thrown gravel over the mess to tidy it up. That patch was smooth, firm and free of dust, while the road around it was not.

Hooley worked out a recipe: heat tar, mix it with crushed stone and slag (a stony waste left over from making iron), spread it, and roll it flat. He applied for a patent in 1902 and set up a company in 1903 called Tar Macadam (Purnell Hooley's Patent) Syndicate Limited. He was a better engineer than businessman and struggled to sell it. In 1905 an ironworks owner and Member of Parliament, Sir Alfred Hickman, took over the business and relaunched it under a short, catchy name: Tarmac. The company still exists today, and many people in Britain call any black road surface 'tarmac'.

Other surfaces joined in. Asphalt, a sticky black material made from the heavy leftovers of crude oil, was mixed with sand and stone to make a smooth, quiet road, and modern mixed asphalt paving became common in the 1920s. Concrete was harder and lasted longer, and in America it became a favourite for main highways. Most roads today are still asphalt or concrete, laid on carefully drained layers of crushed stone, just as McAdam taught.

sections.heading: Coast to Coast: The Lincoln Highway and Route 66
paragraphs: Smooth town streets were one thing. Crossing a whole continent was another. In 1912 the United States had no proper road from coast to coast. Beyond the big eastern cities, drivers found a maze of farm tracks, river crossings and desert trails, and often navigated by following telephone poles.

Carl G. Fisher (1874–1939) wanted to change that. Fisher was an energetic businessman from Indiana who had made a fortune selling car headlights and had helped build the Indianapolis Motor Speedway. In September 1912 he proposed a 'coast-to-coast rock highway', an improved road all the way from New York to San Francisco, and he hoped it would be ready by May 1915 for a big world's fair in San Francisco. He guessed it would cost about 10 million dollars and asked car companies and drivers to donate. Within a month friends had promised a million.

The Lincoln Highway Association was founded on 1 July 1913, with Henry B. Joy, president of the Packard car company, as its leader, and naming the road after Abraham Lincoln gave it a patriotic feel. The route ran from Times Square in New York City to Lincoln Park in San Francisco, through 13 states, and its first official length was 3,389 miles (5,454 km).

At the start, the Lincoln Highway was more of an idea than a road. Less than half of it was improved. The association's own scouting trip in 1913 took 34 days and met mud, sand drifts, overheated engines, floods and broken axles. So the association came up with a clever trick to persuade people. From 1914 it paid for 'seedling miles', short demonstration stretches of smooth concrete road in the middle of muddy countryside. The first was finished in November 1914 near Malta, Illinois. Once local drivers had felt how wonderful a mile of concrete was, the idea went, they would demand that the rest of the road be paved too. It worked: towns and states gradually improved their sections, and red, white and blue stripes painted on poles marked the route.

In 1926 the United States brought order to its growing jumble of named trails by giving main roads numbers instead. East–west routes got even numbers and north–south routes got odd numbers. Much of the Lincoln Highway became US 30. And on 11 November 1926 a brand-new number was born: US Route 66.

Route 66 ran about 2,448 miles (3,940 km) from Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California, through eight states. Unlike most highways, it did not run straight; it curved diagonally across the country, linking many small towns in Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico and Arizona. A promoter from Oklahoma named Cyrus Avery pushed hard for it. In 1938 it became the first US highway to be completely paved from end to end.

Route 66 became famous for the people who travelled it. In the 1930s, during the Great Depression and the terrible dust storms of the 'Dust Bowl', tens of thousands of poor farming families from Oklahoma and nearby states drove west on it, hoping for work in California. The writer John Steinbeck called it 'the mother road' in his 1939 novel The Grapes of Wrath. After World War II it became a road of holidays and adventure, lined with diners, motels and gas stations with bright neon signs, as you will see in Part 14.

sections.heading: Sixty-Two Days in the Mud: Eisenhower's Convoy
paragraphs: Imagine it is the summer of 1919 and World War I has just ended. The US Army wants to know: could it move soldiers and supplies across America by truck? So it organises a test, a long line of military vehicles called a convoy, from Washington, D.C., to San Francisco.

On 7 July 1919 the convoy set off. It was huge: 81 vehicles and trailers, including many heavy cargo trucks, stretched out in a long line along the road. About 24 expeditionary officers, 15 observers from the War Department and 258 enlisted soldiers went along. One of those observers was a 28-year-old lieutenant colonel named Dwight D. Eisenhower, who joined the convoy at its first night's stop in Frederick, Maryland. He later said he went 'partly for a lark, and partly to learn.'

He learned a lot. For much of the way the convoy followed the Lincoln Highway, and the farther west it went, the worse things got. In Nebraska, Wyoming and Utah the roads were often mud or sand. Trucks sank and had to be dragged out with winches and ropes. The convoy broke dozens of old wooden bridges, 14 of them in Wyoming alone, and soldiers had to repair them before the trucks could cross. In the Utah and Nevada desert, the 'road' was sometimes little more than a track. Altogether the convoy stopped about 230 times for breakdowns, repairs, accidents and stuck vehicles.

The planners had hoped the convoy would move much faster. In fact it managed only about 5.65 mph (about 9 km/h), roughly the speed of a fast jog, over more than 3,200 miles. The trip took 62 days: 56 days of travel and six days of rest. The convoy rolled into Oakland, California, on 5 September 1919, a few days behind schedule, and crossed the bay by ferry into San Francisco the next morning, where crowds cheered.

In his official report, Eisenhower wrote plainly that long truck journeys across the middle of the country were 'impracticable until roads are improved.' He never forgot the experience. Twenty-five years later, as the top Allied commander in Europe during World War II, he saw something very different in defeated Germany: wide, fast motorways called autobahns. Those two memories, the muddy convoy and the smooth autobahn, would one day help shape the biggest road-building project in history. As he later put it, 'Germany had made me see the wisdom of broader ribbons across the land.'

sections.heading: Roads Only for Cars: Autobahns and Interstates
paragraphs: Even a well-paved road had a problem once cars became common. It was shared by everyone: walkers, cyclists, horses, farm carts, children and cows, with crossroads and driveways every few metres. A fast car could not safely go fast. Engineers began to dream of a completely new kind of road: one only for motor vehicles, with no crossroads at the same level, separate lanes for each direction, and gentle curves designed for speed. Today we call these motorways, freeways or expressways.

One early experiment was the AVUS in Berlin, a 10 km road with separate carriageways, begun in 1913 and finally opened in 1921 as a racetrack and testing road. In 1926 a German group called HAFRABA began planning a motorway from Hamburg through Frankfurt to Basel in Switzerland. Its detailed plans filled 70 volumes, but it could not get the money or political support to build it.

Germany's first true section of road of this kind ran between the cities of Cologne and Bonn. It was about 18 to 20 km long, built from 1929 to 1932 partly to give work to unemployed men during a terrible economic crisis, and it was strongly supported by Cologne's mayor, Konrad Adenauer. It opened to traffic on 6 August 1932, a few months before the Nazis came to power. (Officially it was classed as a country road at first, and only got full autobahn status in 1958.)

After Adolf Hitler took power in 1933, the Nazi government took over the motorway idea and pretended it had been Hitler's own. A huge national network, the Reichsautobahn, was announced, and Hitler was filmed and photographed turning the first spade of earth near Frankfurt in September 1933. Those pictures were used endlessly in propaganda, the use of news, films and posters to persuade people, to make the regime look modern and caring. The reality was harsher. Workers were paid little, worked 11 to 12 hours a day, and suffered many accidents, and as time went on, prisoners and forced labourers were made to work on the roads. The first completed stretch, Frankfurt to Darmstadt, opened in May 1935. About 3,000 km were finished by the end of 1938, and roughly 3,800 km when work stopped in 1941. Germany had few private cars at the time, so many of these roads were nearly empty.

Now go back to Eisenhower. In 1953 he became President of the United States. America already had a few modern toll roads, such as the Pennsylvania Turnpike, opened in 1940, but there was no national network, and traffic jams and crashes were growing every year. Eisenhower pushed for a giant plan, and on 29 June 1956 he signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act. It authorised about 41,000 miles (66,000 km) of new high-speed roads, called the Interstate Highway System, to be built over roughly ten years. The first estimate of the cost was 25 billion dollars.

How do you pay for that? The law created a Highway Trust Fund, filled by taxes on gasoline, tires and new vehicles. The federal government paid 90 percent of the building costs and each state paid 10 percent, so every tank of fuel helped build the roads it was burned on.

The Interstates had no traffic lights and no level crossroads: you joined and left them only by ramps. Even the numbers followed a pattern. North–south routes got odd numbers, low in the west (I-5 on the Pacific coast) and rising towards the east (I-95 on the Atlantic). East–west routes got even numbers, low in the south (I-10) and higher in the north (I-90).

Building took much longer than ten years. The system was officially declared complete on 14 October 1992, when the last planned section of I-70 opened through the steep Glenwood Canyon in Colorado. Today the Interstate system is nearly 49,000 miles (roughly 78,700 km) long. It is a tiny fraction of America's roads, yet about a quarter of all the miles Americans drive happen on it. As Part 14 will show, though, these mighty roads also cut through cities and neighbourhoods, and not everyone was happy about where they went.

sections.heading: Red, Amber, Green: The Story of Traffic Lights
paragraphs: Traffic lights are older than cars. The very first one was built for horses. In the 1860s the streets around the Houses of Parliament in London were jammed with carriages, carts and people on foot, and crossing the road was dangerous. A railway engineer named John Peake Knight (1828–1886) had an idea. Railways already used signals with moving arms, called semaphores, to tell train drivers to stop or go. Why not use one on the street?

On 9 December 1868 Knight's signal was put up near Westminster Bridge, at the corner of Great George Street and Bridge Street, right outside Parliament. It was a tall pillar with arms that a police constable raised or lowered by hand. Arms straight out meant stop; arms lowered meant drivers could go with care. At night, when the arms were hard to see, the constable used a lever to show a red or green lamp, lit by gas.

For a few weeks it worked. Then, on 2 January 1869, a leak of gas caused one of the lamps to explode, injuring the policeman who was operating it. The signal was taken away, and London did not try the idea again for decades.

The electric light bulb made safe traffic signals possible. In 1912 a police officer in Salt Lake City, Utah, named Lester Wire built an electric traffic light, often described as the first. Two years later, in August 1914, the American Traffic Signal Company installed an electric signal with red and green lights at the corner of East 105th Street and Euclid Avenue in Cleveland, Ohio. It is often called the first electric traffic signal put to regular use on a public street.

There was still something missing. With only red and green, a light could suddenly switch from go to stop and give drivers no warning. In 1920 a Detroit police officer, William Potts, designed a signal with three colours for a four-way crossing, adding an amber (yellow) light between red and green to mean 'caution, the light is about to change.' In 1921 Detroit put up Potts's automatic four-way signals in 15 towers around the city. Soon automatic timers replaced many of the police officers who had worked signals by hand.

Garrett Morgan (1877–1963) is often named as the inventor of the traffic light, but that is not quite right. Morgan was a remarkable African American inventor and businessman in Cleveland. According to his own account, he saw a crash between a car and a horse-drawn carriage, and decided crossings needed a better signal. In 1923 he received US patent number 1,475,024 for a traffic signal: a hand-cranked pole with arms showing 'stop' and 'go', and an extra position that could stop traffic in every direction at once so that people could cross safely, rather like the 'all-red' moment many traffic lights still use. He later sold the rights to General Electric for 40,000 dollars. His signal was an important improvement, but earlier signals existed from 1868 and electric ones from 1914.

sections.heading: Rules of the Road
paragraphs: Once cars were common, everyone needed to follow the same rules. Some of the earliest rules were made in Britain, which, as Part 2 told, had very strict speed limits for road locomotives. In January 1896 those limits were still in force, and they were painfully slow: 2 mph in towns.

On 28 January 1896 a man named Walter Arnold drove his Benz car through East Peckham, a village in Kent, in southeast England. He was going about 8 mph (13 km/h), roughly four times the town limit and about as fast as a person can jog. A policeman chased him down, reportedly on a bicycle, and Arnold was taken to court. He was fined one shilling, plus costs. He is believed to be the first person ever convicted of speeding. Later that same year the law changed and the speed limit rose to 14 mph, and in 1903 a new Motor Car Act raised it to 20 mph.

Driving licences began with the very first cars. In 1888, after people in the town complained about the noise and smell of his Motorwagen, Karl Benz received written permission from the authorities of the Grand Duchy of Baden to drive on public roads. Britain made driving licences compulsory from 1 January 1904, with a minimum age of 17, but you did not have to pass a test: you simply applied. Compulsory driving tests in Britain only came with the Road Traffic Act of 1934. In the United States, New York required licences for professional drivers (chauffeurs) from 1910, and in 1913 New Jersey became the first state to make every driver pass an exam.

Number plates, or licence plates, let the police identify a car. France led the way: an order from the Paris police on 14 August 1893 is usually counted as the start of registration plates. Germany followed in 1896 and the Netherlands created the first national plates in 1898, numbered simply 1, 2, 3 and so on. In New York, from 1901, car owners had to show their initials on the back of the car, and many motorists made their own plates from leather or metal. Massachusetts became the first American state to hand out official plates, in 1903.

Road signs had to be invented too. In 1914 or 1915 a Detroit police sergeant named Harry Jackson cut the corners off a square board and painted the word STOP on it, and Michigan began using stop signs in 1915. The first ones were black letters on white, about 60 cm (24 inches) square. In 1922 American highway officials picked the eight-sided octagon shape, so drivers could recognise a stop sign even from behind or when it was covered in snow. Strangely, for years stop signs were yellow, because red paint that did not fade in sunlight was hard to make. Only in 1954 did the familiar white letters on red become the American standard, matching the red of traffic lights. Many countries agreed on similar shapes and colours at the Vienna Convention on Road Signs and Signals in 1968.

Then there is the biggest rule of all: which side of the road do you drive on? Nobody knows for sure why some places chose left and others right; popular stories about sword arms or Napoleon have no solid evidence behind them. A London law of 1756 told carriages on London Bridge to keep left, and Britain stayed on the left. Massachusetts made driving on the right law in 1821, and when Ford's Model T put the steering wheel on the left in 1908, other American carmakers soon followed. Today about 75 countries and territories, home to about a third of the world's people, drive on the left. Sweden switched from left to right on Sunday 3 September 1967, a day called Dagen H, when every driver stopped, carefully crossed to the other side and set off again.

sections.heading: Fill Her Up! The First Filling Stations
paragraphs: The last thing roads needed was fuel. In Part 5, Bertha Benz bought her fuel, a cleaning liquid called ligroin, from a pharmacy in Wiesloch in 1888. For years after that, drivers bought petrol in cans from pharmacies, hardware stores, bicycle shops and blacksmiths, and poured it into the tank through a funnel. It was messy, slow and dangerous: spilled fuel could easily catch fire.

The answer was a building made just for selling fuel. In 1905 one of the earliest purpose-built filling stations opened in St. Louis, Missouri, at 420 South Theresa Avenue. In 1907 the Standard Oil Company of California opened one in Seattle. Early stations were often just a shed, a storage tank and a hose, with an attendant who filled your car for you.

Soon stations became welcoming places where drivers could pull in off the street. Standard Oil of Ohio opened a drive-in station in Columbus in 1912. In December 1913 the Gulf Refining Company opened a smart brick station in Pittsburgh, designed by an architect. It sold fuel and oil, offered air for tires, had restrooms, and handed out free road maps, which became a tradition at American gas stations for decades. Other countries followed: Britain's first, run by the Automobile Association, opened at Aldermaston in 1919. Self-service, where drivers fill up their own cars, did not become common in the United States until after a station in Los Angeles tried it in 1947.

So much had to be invented besides the car itself: smooth surfaces, long highways, motorways, traffic lights, licences, number plates, stop signs and filling stations. By the 1960s and 1970s, shiny new highways stretched to the horizon. Families began loading suitcases, picnic baskets and children into the back seat to see where those roads would take them, and, as the next part shows, the car was about to change not just how people travelled, but where and how they lived.

deepDive: Road-building is a story about money and who pays. McAdam's roads were paid for by turnpike tolls, which is why early motorists and cyclists in Britain and America campaigned for public road funding in the 'Good Roads' movement. The US took a big step with the Federal Aid Road Act of 1916, which offered federal money to states that set up highway departments, and an even bigger one in 1956, when the Highway Trust Fund turned fuel tax into a dedicated road budget. The 90/10 split meant states could build huge projects for a small share of the cost, which strongly encouraged building, sometimes faster than communities could debate where roads should go. Historians still argue about how much Germany's autobahns inspired the Interstates. Eisenhower himself pointed to both his 1919 convoy and the autobahns, but American engineers had been planning toll-free 'interregional highways' since the late 1930s, and the 1956 law grew out of reports written before he took office. The Nazi myth that the autobahn was Hitler's idea has also been taken apart: the HAFRABA plans and the Cologne–Bonn road came first, and the regime's claims that autobahns ended unemployment were exaggerated, since direct employment peaked at about 125,000 workers in 1936. Traffic lights raise their own engineering questions. A simple fixed-time signal wastes time when roads are empty, so engineers added detectors buried in the road, then computers that coordinate whole corridors so cars meet a 'green wave'. Modern signals use sensors and cameras to adapt timing every few seconds. Even the colours involve physics and psychology: red has the longest wavelength of visible light, scatters least in fog and was already the railway signal for danger, so it was a natural choice for 'stop'. Today's debate is about who roads are for. Many cities are reconsidering wide urban highways, and some, like Syracuse in New York, plan to replace elevated freeways with street-level boulevards.
funFact: For about 30 years, from 1924 to 1954, American stop signs were yellow, because red paint that would not fade in the sun was hard to make.

check.q: Who was the first person known to be convicted of speeding, and how fast was he going?
check.a: Walter Arnold, about 8 mph, in Kent, England, in 1896
wrong: Henry Ford, about 60 mph, in Detroit in 1908
Bertha Benz, about 30 mph, in Germany in 1888
John Peake Knight, about 20 mph, in London in 1868
